en: Title: *Nirvikalpastuti* Author: Rāhulabhadra Source:

Kaiser Library Manuscript 197 = NGMPP C 21/7 (note rare folios here, standardized); for another edition, see Michael Hahn, “Bemerkungen zu zwei Texten aus dem Phudrag-Kanjur,” in Helmut Eimer (ed.), *Indology and Indo-Tibetology: Thirty Years of Indian and Indo-Tibetan Studies in Bonn*, Indica et Tibetica 13. Bonn: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1988, pp. 53–80.
Siddham. Homage to the Blessed Noble Perfection of Wisdom!

Homage to you, O immeasurable Prajñāpāramitā, who are free from conceptual construction; you whose every limb is entirely faultless are beheld by those who are themselves without fault. Like space, you are untainted, free from conceptual proliferation, and beyond syllables.

But he who beholds you with true devotion, he beholds the Tathāgata. O Noble One, endowed as you are with virtues, the virtuous perceive no difference between you and the Buddha, the Teacher of the World, just as none exists between the moon and its moonlight.
Those whose nature is compassion, having approached you who are preceded by the Buddha and the Dharma, attain incomparable greatness with ease, O you who are fond of devotion.
Even one who, with a pure intention, beholds you according to the prescribed rite even once—
By him as well, success is certainly attained when seeing her whose vision is unfailing;
this is true for all heroes who have restrained their minds for the sake of others and whose souls are devoted to the welfare of others.
You are the nurse and the biological mother, full of affection for us. Since the Buddhas, the compassionate teachers of the world, are your sons,
you are therefore auspicious, the grandmother of all sentient beings.
You too, O auspicious and blameless Hahn, are always followed by all the stainless perfections (pāramitās), just as the crescent moon is followed by the stars. [8]
Having encountered those to be trained here and there, you alone, though one, are praised by the Tathāgatas under various names in many forms—
just as droplets of dew, having encountered the blazing light of the sun, are transformed.
Having reached you, the faults and the disputations of disputants go to their dissolution.
You alone, appearing terrible, generate terror in the ignorant; yet you, appearing serene, generate consolation for the wise.
O Mother, how could passion and hatred arise in anyone else for one whose Master has no attachment even toward you?
You do not come from anywhere, nor do you go anywhere at all.
Furthermore, you are not perceived by the wise even in all places [where you might be expected].
Yet those who do not see you at all take refuge in you with devotion;
having taken refuge, they are liberated—this is a great marvel! [13–14]
Beholding you alone, one is bound; not beholding you, one is also bound.
Beholding you alone, one is liberated; not beholding you, one is also liberated.
Oh, how wondrous you are! How profound you are! How glorious you are!
You are exceedingly difficult to understand; like an illusion, you are seen and yet you are not seen.
You are cultivated by the Buddhas, the Pratyekabuddhas, and the Śrāvakas;
you alone are the path to liberation—there is no other, this is certain.
Out of compassion for embodied beings, the Lords of the World, having prioritized conventional usage, speak of you for the sake of designation, yet they also do not speak of you. [18]
Who here is capable of praising you, who are without cause, stainless,
beyond the scope of all speech, and who are never dependent on anything?
Even so, for the sake of conventional reality, we shall do so with such paths of words as these.
Though you are beyond praise, we are deeply satisfied in our desire to extol you. By whatever merit I have accumulated through praising the Perfection of Wisdom,
may the entire world swiftly become devoted to the Perfection of Wisdom.
Thus ends the Praise of the Non-conceptual.
May there be auspiciousness at all times and in all places for all sentient beings.
